sections.text: Introduction

SF6 gas-filled switching equipment is
now in widespread use throughout EEA's transmission
and distribution system.

This type of equipment can be expected to experience a gradual
loss of SF6 gas due to
normal leakage and occasionally, a larger, more 
rapid gas loss as a result of equipment failure

For these situations a reliable supply of replacement SF6
gas is required.
Directives

Physical Properties of Sulpher
Hexa Fluoride

Pure SF6 is an inert, colorless, odorless, 
non-toxic gas, approx. five times heavier than air.

It is highly stable both chemically and thermally and is
non-flammable.

At normal atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature SF6
is gaseous but will liquefy at relatively high temperature when subjected to
high pressure.

When pressurized above 18 bars the gas will liquefy at normal
ambient temperature.

properties.

that of air at the same pressure and exceeds that of insulating oil.
The dielectric strength increases as gas pressure is increased

sections.text: Storage of SF6 Cylinders

SF6 is normally supplied in 50 kg quantity inside standard steel
cylinders. The cylinders must be stored in accordance with EEA's rules and
regulations for pressurized gas containers.

Cylinders must be stored in an upright position and secured by
chains to prevent them from falling over.

The control valves of the storage cylinders must always be
covered by a protective cap that is securely screwed into its proper position.

Cylinders must 
be stored in a well-ventilated area, protected from direct sunlight and moisture

Large bulk storage cylinders are usually stored on their sides
in specially designed storage racks inside GIS buildings.

sections.text: Gas Handling

SF6 is usually received from the manufacturer in liquid form in
standard gas cylinders. The pressure will vary from 7 bars to 35 bars depending
on the temperature.

Since the pressure within the cylinder is dependent on the
temperature, the quantity of SF6 in the cylinder cannot be measured by the
pressure gauge.

The best indication of remaining contents inside the cylinder
can be obtained by weighing the cylinder and subtracting the empty cylinder tare
weight.

The safe removal of gaseous SF6 from the cylinders requires the
use of a reliable, single stage pressure regulator with a delivery pressure
range of 0 bar to 10 bars.

In order to remove the SF6 in gaseous form, it is necessary to
evaporate the liquid inside the cylinder.

This process must be done very slowly to avoid a rapid
temperature drop due to the evaporation of a gas from liquid state to gaseous
state.

Gas Removal from Gas Insulated Switchgear 
Compartments

During work on internal components of gas-insulated switch-ear,
it is necessary to remove the SF6 from the compartment to be maintained.

Since it is wasteful to vent the gas to atmosphere it is usual
practice to pump it out of the compartment and store it in an S176 gas service
cart for reuse.

This gas service cart has facilities for drying and filtering
the gas when it is returned to the switchgear.

There are no known restrictions on the disposal of
uncontaminated SF6 by discharge into the
atmosphere, but for economic reasons this practice should be avoided.

sections.text: PROXICITY

SF6, in both pure and commercial
grades, is physiologically inert. It has no adverse effects when inhaled at high
concentrations (in air) or for prolonged periods of time.

SF6 contains no oxygen and therefore
will not support life, making it unsafe to work in any unventilated
building containing SF6. Furthermore SF6 is heavier than air and will displace
air in confined areas.

When exposed to sustained or intense electric arcs, SF6
decomposes to form Sulphur-Flourine gases and
metallic fluorides. If moisture is also present, the decomposition product may
include Sulphur - Oxy Fluorides and hydrofluoric acid.

These byproducts, especially hydrofluoric acid, can cause
irritation to the respiratory system and to the eyes.

Fortunately, these compounds possess a very strong smell similar
to rotten eggs and can therefor readily be detected. These gaseous byproducts
can be dispersed easily using suitable forced ventilation.

sections.text: Removal and Disposal of Solid Decomposition Products

The production of gaseous contaminants in sF6 may - in some
cases - be accompanied by the formation of metallic fluorides; however this can
only happen in compartments in which along term partial discharge or an internal
severe power fault has occurred or possibly, inside a circuit breaker which has
been subjected to repeated short circuit fault clearing operations.

Any Powdery deposits found upon opening a SF6 gas compartment
must be treated as metallic fluorides. This powder must be removed promptly,
using efficient vacuum cleaners, since the Powder will quickly absorb moisture
and become corrosive.

During the removal of these powders the technician shall wear
disposable coveralls and gloves and shall be protected by a full-face mask
respirator with filler.

sections.text: Additional Safety Precautions

SF6 gas used in switchgear and other
equipment is always under pressure Circuit
breakers and. gas filled compartments should be considered as pressure vessels.
Inspection and other access covers must not be removed until the internal
pressure has been reduced to atmospheric pressure.

SF6 gas is heavier than air and it will tend to collect at
low point of buildings, in basements and cable vaults, displacing the air in
that area. This can become very dangerous to personnel entering these areas
since it could lead to oxygen starvation and possible suffocation. It is
advisable to use a SF6 detector to detect the
presence of SF6 gas in such areas. Forced ventilation
may be used to purge the areas prior to entering.

In the unlikely event of an internal fault, which ruptures or
burns through the enclosure, extra precautions should be taken to avoid exposure
to the arc decomposition products. The faulted equipment must be approached with
caution and if the strong smell of hydrofluoric acid
is present, the immediate area should be evacuated and thoroughly vented until
the odor subsides.
